text: State, step, stop: worked simulation problems.
A simulation has no clever trick. The difficulty is reading **every rule** correctly and turning it into code without slips.
Before coding: list every rule from the statement, note the edge cases (empty input, ties, wrap around), and check the output format character by character.
State: the two scores of the current game. Step: one character. Stop: one side reaches the target **and** leads by 2; the input ends at 'E'.
Store the input once, then run the same function for both rule sets, 11 and 21. Print the last, unfinished game even when it is 0:0 (P1042).
`cin >> ch` skips spaces and line breaks, which is exactly right here: the record can be split over many lines.
Number the seats 0 … n − 1. Moving s seats round the circle is `(p + s) % n` one way and `(p - s + n) % n` the other.
Facing in or out flips left and right. Instead of four cases, "facing direction equals instruction" always means the same way round: one comparison decides it (P1563).
`p - s` can be negative and % keeps the sign: add n first. If s can exceed n, reduce it with `s % n`.
Copy a rule table from the statement into a 2D array once. Then every round is a **lookup**, not a chain of ifs (P1328).
A pattern of length k that repeats forever: round i uses element `i % k`.

Grid simulations (P2670, P4924, P1518) reuse chapter 5's tools: dx and dy arrays, bounds checks, rotating into a second array. If a walk might never end, stop after a safe maximum or detect a repeated state.
Split the output into small decisions, one per rule: sign, coefficient, variable, power. Each decision is one if that matches one sentence of the statement (P1067).

rows: x, not x^1; nothing for x^0

text: String expansion (P1098) and work scheduling (P1065) are the same style: many small rules, each a separate, testable piece.
Add, subtract, multiply and divide numbers stored digit by digit.
long long stops at about 9.2 × 10¹⁸. Longer numbers are kept as a vector of digits, **ones digit first**.

Every operation is the school method: work from the ones digit up, keep a carry or borrow, and remove leading zeros at the end. Read as a string, convert with toBig, compute, trim, print from the last index down.
Loop while either number has digits left **or** there is a carry. Each step: digit sum + carry; keep `% 10`, pass `/ 10` on (P1601).
Numbers of different lengths need no padding: a missing digit counts as 0.
Compare first: more digits means bigger; equal length, compare from the top digit down. Subtract the smaller from the larger, and add a minus sign if you swapped.
Borrow: when a digit goes negative, add 10 and take 1 from the next digit. trim afterwards, so 1000 − 999 prints 1, not 0001.

title: Multiplying by a small number, and factorials

text: Multiplying by an ordinary int k touches each digit once: `digit × k + carry`. The final carry can be several digits long, so push them one by one.
`digit * k + carry` must fit in an int: fine for k up to about 10⁸. For bigger k use long long, or big × big.
Combine the pieces: keep the running factorial and the running sum. Each round is one small multiplication and one big addition (P1009).
Build each value from the previous one, k! = (k − 1)! × k, instead of recomputing from scratch. The same habit makes 2ᵖ cheap (P1045).
Digit i of a times digit j of b lands in **column i + j**. Add all products first, in long long, then sweep the carries once.
A product has at most len(a) + len(b) digits; trim removes the rest, so 0 × 12345 prints 0 (P1303). Cost: O(len(a) × len(b)).
Long division goes the other way, **from the top digit down**: bring down one digit into the remainder, write the quotient digit, keep the remainder.
Only the remainder is needed for "is this huge number divisible by k?". The digit count of 2ᵖ is ⌊p · log₁₀ 2⌋ + 1 (P1045).
Classic C solutions use fixed int arrays with a separate length, read digits with scanf into a char array, and clear arrays with memset.
A fixed array must be big enough for the longest answer: len(a) + len(b) + 1 digits for a product. A vector grows by itself.
